entry.title: 從電信業到資安外商：一場轉職震撼教育
entry.content:
在趨勢科技待了快三個月，這段時間最深刻的體悟就是——我正在經歷一場全方位的「砍掉重練」。

開頭先自我聲明：為了保護讀者，這篇文章會先封印我在外商環境被植入的「晶晶體」。我希望這個網誌能是一個自由的空間，不管是技術、職場牢騷還是中英混雜的心情，都隨當下的狀態而定，看我當下想不想練習一下英文。

之所以重啟這個網站，是受到了我的 Mentor Yu-Jun 的啟發。看著他持續經營自己的網站，我才意識到對於工程師來說，這不僅是筆記，更是一種個人紀錄與專業的「數位資產累積」。

1. 關於「自律」的文化衝擊

外面常開玩笑說趨勢是假外商，但對比我待過的傳統電信業，這裡的文化衝擊依然巨大。

在前公司，即便努力朝向「科技電信業」轉型，但在資源分配與體制下，難免讓人感到疲憊。來到這裡後，我見識到了什麼叫真正的「成果導向」。

在這裡，可以看到一個能力好的員工 10 點多才上班，中午吃飯泡咖啡聊天搞了兩三個小時，下午 4、5 點跑去烤麵包或烤地瓜也沒人會管你，同事們還會很開心的加入。只要你能如期、高品質地交付工作，這些「自由」都是被尊重的。這也意味著，你需要極高的自律、自我技能提升，以及不斷學習的狀態。

2. PR 的三十道陰影：什麼叫嚴謹？

技術面是我挫折感最大的來源。以前覺得專案管理（Jira + Bitbucket）已經行之有年，但在純軟體產業面前，那真的差太多了。

從 SPEC 的定義、詳盡的 POC 到 Design Review，每一階段都是靈魂拷問。最震撼的莫過於 Code Review。以前發 PR 可能只是走個過場，但在這裡，發 PR 是一件嚴肅到近乎神聖的事情。從程式架構、效能優化到甚至是你的 PR Message，任何細節都會被同事刁。

曾有一次 PR 被留了 30 個 Comments，那種挫折感讓我深刻意識到：過去的任何經驗在這一刻並無幫助。我現在需要專注衝刺的，是學好 Golang、學會如何做 Design Review、學會如何做出一場好的 Presentation。

3. 另一個巨大的衝擊是「人」

在會議中，聽著同事用流利的英文與外國團隊溝通，看著周遭超過一半的人不是台大畢業就是留美歸國。對比自己所謂的「台灣野雞大學」背景，那種實力與學歷的差距是實打實的。

這認真啟發了我近期加強英文的決心，我已經開始在尋找美語補習班與線上課程，不想在未來的協作中，因為語言限制了技術的發揮。

4. 成長

最近我也在協助專案導入 datamodel-code-generator。這是一個能透過 Data Model 自動生成 OpenAPI (Swagger) YAML Spec 的工具，能極大地減少手動同步規格的錯誤，之後我會專門寫一篇文章談談細節。

我希望在這裡能越挫越勇。雖然現在 PR 被留 30 個留言，但我相信，總有一天我能挑戰「一次發 PR 就過」。到那天，我一定會再發一篇文章慶祝。

這是一個紀錄我如何從零開始，在資安叢林裡生存並成長的起點。

entry.title: From Chaos to Executive Meetings: How Meeting Minutes Became My Career Shield
entry.content:
Looking back at a chaotic period at my former company, Taiwan Mobile, we experienced a major internal software transition. The company decided to unceremoniously retire Skype and issued a “mandate” from executives requiring all employees to use our in-house messenger, M Plus, for internal communication.

I understand the vision that a great product “needs” its own employees to be “happy users”. However, the sudden sunsetting of Skype caused significant friction, especially since early versions of M+ lacked basic features like cloud recording. But it was exactly this chaos—where re-watching meeting recordings felt like a waste of time—that forced me to develop the habit of writing Meeting Minutes. Little did I know, this would become the most critical pivot in my early career.

1. Survival in Chaos: Blind Typing and Key Extraction

During the era when M+ was still immature, I developed a competitive advantage: Blind Typing Speed.

I made it a habit to record key points and decisions the moment I heard them. If I encountered an uncertain detail, I’d jot down keywords and immediately clarify with colleagues right after the meeting. Over time, I realized I rarely needed to review recordings to produce a comprehensive summary. This not only reinforced my memory but also saved me hours of post-meeting digestion.

2. My Minutes Framework: Making Accountability “Stick”

A powerful set of meeting minutes is never a transcript; it’s a contract. I structured mine into four rigorous sections:

  1. Follow-up on Previous Items: Ensuring every pending task has an update.
  2. Business Unit Progress Reports: Synchronizing the latest status across teams.
  3. Meeting Conclusions: Solidifying consensus to prevent “he-said-she-said” later.
  4. Action Items: Explicitly listing the Owner and Deadline.

Example: IT Group to track project [X] progress and provide feedback to [Y] Group by March 15th.

Once these minutes were distributed—whether to the A Team, the B Office, or the C Office—accountability was crystal clear. It served as the recap for the next meeting and, more importantly, as my ultimate leverage and self-defense mechanism in cross-departmental collaborations.

3. From a 2-Year Rookie to Hosting Executive Briefings

I never expected that a skill many dismiss as “busy work” would earn me such recognition.

My managers were deeply impressed by my ability to organize complex information and synthesize logic. This directly led to me—a young professional with only two years of experience—being appointed as the TPM for a large-scale project for the Ministry of Digital Affairs, and even hosting work briefings for Director-level executives.

When standing before high-level management, my documentation skills kept me grounded. I knew the “why” behind every decision and exactly who was responsible for what.

Minutes are Discipline, and Discipline is Leverage

Meeting minutes are not just for others; they are a manifestation of internal self-discipline. They protect you from finger-pointing in complex projects and ensure your organizational skills are visible to leadership.

A great software engineer doesn’t just manage code; they manage consensus.

Note: I plan to share more about the specific challenges and mindset of hosting Director-level briefings in a future post.

entry.title: From Telepathic Development to Contract-Oriented: Why Spec and Unit Tests are Life Savers
entry.content:
Looking back at my time in my previous company, the development environment was quite “wild.” We lacked formal development standards—even PEP8, Linters, or Formatters were only reluctantly introduced in the later stages of projects. At that time, our most hardcore way of communicating was simply looking at the Database.

Back then, there was no such thing as an API Spec. The only intersection between front-end and back-end developers was:

“Hey, I’ve opened the new fields for that feature in the UserStatus table.”
“The type is VARCHAR(10), go ahead and connect to it yourself.”

We treated the database as the “Source of Truth,” completely ignoring the massive deviations that can occur when different program logics interpret the same data.

1. A Painful Lesson: When “Booleans” Become a Mystery

Without a defined Spec, development is like playing an expensive guessing game. One example that stands out is the definition of a status field.

During our verbal discussion, everyone agreed it was a simple toggle concept. However, when it came to implementation:

  • Back-end Engineer: Intuitively returned a Boolean True / False.
  • Front-end Engineer: Based on past experience, wrote the logic to expect strings "Y" / "N".

The result? The front-end display was permanently broken. Both sides sat staring at the screen during debugging: “I thought we agreed it would be like this…” This kind of low-level error caused by a communication breakdown is exactly why a standard OpenAPI Spec is needed as a development contract.

2. OpenAPI Spec: No More Relying on Intuition

To avoid the tragedies mentioned above, defining a clear YAML document is the first step. It defines not only types but also formats and Enums.

3. Beyond Specs, Why Do We Need Unit Tests?

While Specs solve external communication issues, internal logic correctness relies on Unit Tests.
Many people feel that writing tests is a waste of time. In reality, unit tests are meant to catch those “I thought it was fine” moments. A good test shouldn’t just check the “Happy Path”; it should rigorously verify the following scenarios:

  1. Happy Path: Ensuring the system works as expected when input is correct.
  2. Edge Cases:
  • What happens if the API receives a null value?
  • What happens if a string length exceeds the VARCHAR limit set in the DB?
  1. Boundary Testing:
  • Does the logic collapse when a numerical value is 0 or negative?
  • How does the system behave when an array length is exactly at its upper or lower limit?

Comprehensive unit tests give us the confidence (the “bottom line”) to refactor or add new features without breaking existing ones.

From Writing Code to Building Stable Systems

Moving from having zero standards to learning to write the Spec before starting—and thinking about test cases before writing logic—has been the biggest shift in my development mindset. The Spec is a commitment to the outside world; Unit Testing is self-discipline for the inside.
Good software engineering isn’t about who writes code the fastest; it’s about who can ensure the system remains stable and maintainable one, or even three years down the road.
